newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia hopes for better terms on new borrowing.
newsitem.headline: Croatia hopes for better terms on new borrowing.

text.p: Croatia, granted its first loan from foreign banks on Thursday, said the country's improved position paved the way for future borrowing at better terms on international capital markets.
"The interest rate is very favourable, considering Croatia hasn't got a credit rating," Finance Minister Bozo Prka told reporters. "But we expect it to be even better in the future."
Croatia signed an agreement with some 30 foreign commercial creditor banks for its first 200 million marks ($130 million) syndicated loan, repayable in two years.
The loan was granted at 1.75 percentage points above Libor.
The syndication was substantially oversubscribed, allowing Croatia to raise the target for the borrowing from the original 150 million marks.
The managing director of arranger Dresdner Bank of Luxembourg, Wolfgang Baertz, said both the amount and the price represented an "important benchmark for Croatia".
Government officials said they hoped the country's relatively low debt exposure and good record as a borrower would encourage international investors.
They cited a low fiscal deficit, which was expected to fall below a projected 2-2.5 percent of gross domestic product, and steady economic growth as guaranteeing solid servicing for future debts.
Croatia's gross domestic product was forecast to rise some seven percent in real terms to around 100 billion kuna ($18.5 billion) in 1996 after a more modest increase last year.
Officials hope fresh loans will be given for a longer term. Croatia also plans to tap the Eurobond market later this year after getting a credit rating from leading agencies.
Thanks to lower political risk and a stable macroeconomic situation, it aims for an investment grade rating.
The fact that Croatia agreed to take over and repay its portion of the former Yugoslav debt to the so-called London and Paris Clubs of creditors is viewed as very positive, Prka said.

A recent normalisation of relations with neighbouring Serbia -- its enemy in the 1991-95 Balkan conflict -- and a positive role in Bosnian elections to reinforce a fragile peace also improved the country's international image.
